Front: Explain `What is an enum?` deeply enough for review.
Back: An enum defines a fixed set of named constants as a type-safe class-like construct.
Extra: Enums implicitly extend `java.lang.Enum` and cannot extend any other class. They are final by default, cannot be instantiated with `new`, and enforce compile-time type safety over integer constants.

Front: Explain `Declare enum` deeply enough for review.
Back: Enums are declared using the `enum` keyword as top-level or static nested types.
Extra: Enums cannot be declared locally inside methods (prior to Java 16). Nested enums are implicitly static. Example: `public enum Status { PENDING, ACTIVE }`

Front: Explain `Enum constructor` deeply enough for review.
Back: Enum constructors are implicitly private and executed during class initialization for each constant.
Extra: Declaring an enum constructor as `public` or `protected` results in a compile-time error. They cannot be called with `new`. Example: `private Coin(int value) { this.value = value; }`

Front: Explain `Enum field` deeply enough for review.
Back: Enums can define instance or static fields; instance fields should be final.
Extra: Because enum constants are singletons, instance fields should be final/immutable to prevent runtime state pollution. Constant declarations must precede any field/method declarations.

Front: Explain `Enum method` deeply enough for review.
Back: Enums can define static, instance, or abstract methods overridden by each constant.
Extra: Abstract methods are useful for constant-specific behavior. Example: `public enum Op { PLUS { public double apply(double a, double b) { return a+b; } }; public abstract double apply(double a, double b); }`

Back: values() returns an array containing all enum constants in their declaration order.
Extra: The array returned by `values()` is cloned on every call to prevent callers from modifying the enum's internal constants array, causing garbage collection overhead in hot loops.

Back: valueOf(String name) returns the enum constant matching the string exactly.
Extra: The string match is strictly case-sensitive. If no match is found, it throws `IllegalArgumentException`; if the argument is `null`, it throws `NullPointerException`.

Back: ordinal() returns the numerical position of the enum constant starting at 0.
Extra: Avoid using `ordinal()` for database keys or business logic. Reordering or inserting constants changes their ordinals, leading to silent bugs and data corruption.

Back: name() returns the exact string name of the enum constant as declared.
Extra: Unlike `toString()`, `name()` is declared `final` in `java.lang.Enum` and cannot be overridden. Always use `name()` when you need the exact identifier string.

Front: Explain `Enum in switch` deeply enough for review.
Back: Enums can be used in switch statements, requiring unqualified case labels.
Extra: You must use `case SPRING:` instead of `case Season.SPRING:`. If the switched enum variable evaluates to `null`, a `NullPointerException` is thrown before matching starts.

Front: Explain `Enum implements interface` deeply enough for review.
Back: Enums can implement interfaces to allow polymorphic behavior across constants.
Extra: Each constant can implement the interface method individually in its own constant-specific class body, or the enum class can provide a default implementation.

Front: Explain `Enum Singleton pattern` deeply enough for review.
Back: A single-element enum is the safest and simplest way to implement a Singleton.
Extra: Enums provide built-in serialization safety and JVM-level protection against reflection instantiation attacks, which normally plague class-based Singletons. When deserialized, the JVM resolves the instance by name alone, preventing duplicate instances.

Front: Explain how Java prevents reflection instantiation of enums under the hood.
Back: Java reflection blocks enum instantiation at the class constructor level.
Extra: `Constructor.newInstance()` explicitly checks the class modifiers. If the class has the `Modifier.ENUM` flag set, it immediately throws `IllegalArgumentException` with the message "Cannot reflectively create enum objects", preserving instance control.

Front: Explain the advantages of comparing enums using the `==` operator over `.equals()`.
Back: Using `==` is faster, null-safe, and checked at compile time.
Extra: Reference equality (`==`) is null-safe (comparing a null reference to an enum constant evaluates to `false` without throwing `NullPointerException`). It also enforces compile-time type compatibility (comparing two different enum types causes a compile error), whereas `.equals()` accepts any object and returns `false` at runtime.
